# Rectus Abdominis Barely Contracts During Lifting; the Obliques Do the Work, So Add Side-Bending, Heavy Lifting and Twisting

**What it is** — The authors: "Contrary to common belief, the abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis) do not contract to any significant degree during lifting or pushing. Studies of the electrical activity of the stomach show that it is deeper muscles of the stomach (the internal and external obliques) which are much more active during lifting. The apparent hardening of the 'abdominals' on straining is usually caused by passive bulging of these muscles and their sheaths. The one time when the abdominals contract powerfully in the standing position occurs during explosive expulsion of air from the lungs or during backward extension of the torso. This implies that abdominal exercises should be augmented by side-bending, heavy lifting or twisting activities to strengthen all the different muscle groups that contribute to stomach and torso stability" (PDF 479 / p.468, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning is from EMG: if the obliques, not rectus abdominis, are the active trunk muscles under load, exercises that load the obliques (side-bending, twisting) and heavy standing lifts are what train the muscles used. Inference: the "hardening" a lifter feels under strain is pressure pushing the wall out, so it is not evidence that crunch-type work is training the bracing muscles.

**When to apply** — When a trunk programme is built mostly on sit-ups or crunches for an athlete who lifts or pushes: add side-bending, rotational work and heavy standing lifts. When a lifter or coach reads a hard-feeling stomach under load as "abs working."

**When NOT to apply** — The EMG "studies" are not cited on this page, so `untested`. Two exceptions are on the page itself: rectus abdominis does contract powerfully in forceful exhalation and in backward extension of the torso. The point is about lifting and pushing; it does not say rectus abdominis is unimportant for trunk flexion. The 7.4.2 entry adds that the obliques acting bilaterally "augment action by rectus abdominis" in flexion ([[claim--trunk-rotation-is-driven-by-the-obliques-not-the-erector-spinae]]), so the two sections agree that the obliques matter but address different movements.

**Example** — The authors' own exceptions show when rectus abdominis does fire: "during explosive expulsion of air from the lungs or during backward extension of the torso" (PDF 479 / p.468).

**Related** — [[claim--trunk-rotation-is-driven-by-the-obliques-not-the-erector-spinae]] (7.4.2: obliques drive rotation and augment flexion), [[claim--lifting-belt-restrains-abdominal-pressure-and-supports-the-stomach-more-than-the-back]] (the stomach muscles as the internal restraint), [[principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting]]

# "Muscle Isolation" Is Possible Only for Small Muscle Groups at Low Intensity; Heavy or Prolonged Resistance Recruits Stabilisers Until Isolation Is Essentially Impossible

**What it is** — Generations of bodybuilding-magazine authors have advocated specific
machines, joint-fixation methods, precise limb placement and other techniques claimed to
maximally recruit one muscle group while others stay "largely dormant." "EMG studies reveal
that isolation of minute muscle groups is indeed possible under low intensities of loading
(e.g. Basmajian, 1978)": low-intensity actions like eye-blinking, piano-playing or relaxed speech
rely on precise, isolated action of specific small muscle groups. However, once a large load
is imposed on a target muscle group by intense resistance, isolation becomes "virtually
impossible": as soon as the load is applied, stabilising muscles engage to keep the body or
specific joints stable while prime movers cope with the load, and if the nervous system
signals the prime movers are inadequate, assistant movers, shunt muscles, emergency muscles
and neutralisers may all be recruited to help. Physiotherapists using PNF sometimes impose
maximal loading on a joint deliberately to elicit compensatory or overflow activity of
muscles other than the prime movers. "The higher the intensity or the greater the duration
of the exercise, the less likely is isolation of the prime mover, even if certain joints are
restrained as on an isokinetic test machine," and "in many cases the tension developed in
the stabilisers or assistant stabilisers will equal or exceed that of the prime movers." The
authors' worked example: during heavy
standing triceps push-downs on a cable machine, the abdominals, latissimus dorsi and erector
spinae "may be as strongly contracted as the triceps," despite this being nominally a
triceps-isolation exercise; analysis of many seated or reclining "isolation" machine
exercises shows isolation simply does not occur with heavy loads. The authors tie this to the load-dependent
proximal/distal recruitment shift noted earlier in the chapter, which they say shows isolation
under significant resistance is impossible (PDF p. 229, printed p. 218; see
[[claim--muscle-recruitment-consistency-and-proximal-distal-shift-with-load]]), where the
authors explicitly forward-referenced this section. This does not negate the value of
isolation-style exercises: they can be useful in early injury rehabilitation, and the
overflow to other muscle groups at higher loads can itself be desirable (if performed
safely), since it simultaneously offers isometric and dynamic training to those other muscle
groups. The authors' stated purpose for this section is to correct the "misleading concept
of muscle isolation" still promoted by many instructors and training texts. (PDF p. 252,
printed p. 241, "4.2.9 The Concept of Muscle Isolation.")

**Why it works** — The mechanism given is neuromuscular: as load intensity or duration rises, the central
nervous system recruits whatever additional muscle groups (stabilisers, assistant movers,
emergency muscles, neutralisers) are needed to keep the targeted joint and the body stable
and to complete the movement, since a single "isolated" muscle group's own capacity is
insufficient against a heavy load; at low intensities, EMG shows isolation of minute muscle
groups (PDF p. 252, printed p. 241).

**When to apply** — Use this claim to correctly interpret what a "muscle isolation" exercise
is actually training at a given load and duration. EMG shows isolation of minute muscle
groups at low intensity (PDF p. 252, printed p. 241); the authors separately say isolation
exercises can help in the early stages of injury rehabilitation. Inference: low-load rehab
isolation work may approach isolation, but the book does not show it for limb muscles.
Inference: this fits [[claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance]]'s
finding that effort and tension spread between muscle groups. At hypertrophy- or
strength-level heavy or prolonged loading, expect and potentially embrace the overflow to stabilisers and
assistant movers as additional, simultaneous isometric/dynamic training for those muscle
groups rather than treating it as a programming failure.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not describe a heavy-load exercise (a heavy cable push-down, a
heavy leg-extension set) as "isolating" the target muscle group in marketing, coaching cues,
or programme design; per this claim and its EMG evidence, isolation is shown only for minute muscle
groups at low training intensities. Do not assume the specific triceps push-down example
generalises identically to every "isolation" exercise; the authors give it as one worked
illustration, not a universally quantified finding across exercises.

**Example** — The book's own example is the heavy triceps push-down engaging abdominals,
latissimus dorsi and erector spinae described above; no further invented example is added
here.

**Related** — [[claim--muscle-recruitment-consistency-and-proximal-distal-shift-with-load]]
(this chapter's own forward reference to this entry, 4.2.2),
[[claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance]] (Ch3, a related finding
on how tension in one muscle group affects others).

**Also in 8.3** — "In some cases, the stabilising muscles which have not been identified are so strongly contracted that they are being efficiently conditioned at the same time as the prime movers. For example, heavy overhead presses, squats and tricep push downs can produce higher levels of tension in the abdominal muscles (trunk stabilisers) than sit-ups" (PDF 442 / p.431, checked against the page image; no EMG data are given on that page). See [[principle--minimax-principle-of-training-economics]].

# Machine Training Safety: A 24-Point Checklist of Hazards and Countermeasures, and Why Machines Need the Same Supervision as Free Weights

**What it is** — Section 8.10 opens: "It is commonly believed that gymnasium machines are intrinsically safer than free weights and require far less skill in using them. This fallacy is one reason why injuries are still regularly sustained by those who rely solely on machines for training." Machines "must be operated correctly to ensure safety and effectiveness," which needs "an adequate knowledge of the merits, deficiencies and the principles underlying the design of each machine," and of how a machine exercise differs from its free-weight equivalent in "which muscles act as prime movers and stabilisers at all stages of the exercise, as well as which tendons and ligaments are significantly stressed" (PDF 480 / p.469, checked against the page image). The list that follows has 24 bullets (PDF 481-483 / pp.470-472, counted on the page images). Grouped here by hazard (the grouping is this entry's, the items are the authors'):
- **Forced lumbar flexion or rounding**: seated vertical pressing machines (round the lower back, lean forward, hyperextend the lumbar spine; seated pressing loads the lumbar spine "as much as 90% more" than standing, Chaffin & Andersson, 1984, so these are not "basic exercises for novices"); seated leg press (backrests that "do not match the natural curvatures of the spine"; "Never allow the weight to return so rapidly that the momentum forces the lumbar spine to round"); lying inclined or vertical leg press (thighs to abdomen: "carefully limit the range of knee flexion and perform the movement slowly"); calf-raise machines; seated back extension (start flexed, end in "loaded hyperextension"; use "only a small range").
- **Forced lumbar hyperextension**: prone leg curl, flat or rounded (place "a roll of firm sponge rubber or towelling under your hip joint"), and inclined (stabilise the hips "or rather use a standing leg curl or pulley machine"); standing leg raise (shift forward off the backrest, "crunching form of a gymnastics 'pike'"); seated bent-arm pullover ("restricting your range of movement").
- **Weak or vulnerable start positions**: bench press machines ("start from your weakest biomechanical position with the bar at chest level," no pre-stretch: a partner helps you begin from extended elbows); pec decks (shoulder externally rotated at the start: a partner pulls the grips forward); a general bullet naming seated bench press, seated leg press, bench press machine and Smith machine: "always ask a partner to help you begin in a safer position and to 'spot' you."
- **Shear, torsion or extra joint load**: hack squat ("excessive shearing force on the knee ... a poor, unsafe substitute for the free standing squat"); seated spinal twist ("strictly upright posture and severely limit range and speed"); standing spinal or hip twisting machines ("little more than useless for 'trimming the waist'"); standing hip adduction/abduction (simultaneous spinal rotation or flexion/extension); Smith vertical press (a larger load on "the spine, shoulders and wrists" than standing free-weight presses); hyperextension machines (hamstrings, popliteus and knee capsule; the knee "tends to be hyperextended").
- **Trunk and hip flexors**: abdominal machines with heel, calf or thigh grips (rely more on iliopsoas; but "there is nothing intrinsically 'wrong'" with recruiting it, "what may be most risky is the inappropriate timing"); sit-up boards with ankle or foot grips (see [[heuristic--after-foot-anchored-sit-ups-stretch-the-iliopsoas-under-load]]).
- **System-level bullets**: any machine that requires you to sit; seated pressing machines with foot rests that make the hips and lower back hard to stabilise ("keep your feet firmly on the ground"); immobilised joints shifting stress (see [[principle--a-machine-that-immobilises-one-joint-shifts-stress-to-adjacent-joints]]); circuits against the clock; poorly designed, maintained or lubricated machines ("report any such machines to the gym supervisor").

The closing rule: the list "should suffice to increase your awareness that machines are not inherently safer than free weights and that all types of resistance training require learning of the appropriate technical skills for efficiency and safety"; the instructor "should never assume that a client does not need to be closely supervised at all times, even when using machines," because "*continuous observation and spotting are just as important for machines as for free weights exercises* if the safety claims of machine manufacturers are to be realised in practice" (PDF 483 / p.472, italics in the original).

**Why it works** — The authors' recurring mechanism is that a machine fixes the path and the body position, so the user cannot use hips, knees and ankles "to absorb shock or redistribute loading," and "The posture of stable neutral pelvic tilt becomes far more difficult to maintain" (PDF 482 / p.471). Where the machine forces an end-range position or a weak start, the countermeasure is range limits, slower speed, or a partner.

**When to apply** — Auditing a facility's machines, writing a machine circuit for general clients or injured athletes, or briefing new staff. Eric's review: the baseline's operating value is "safety first, keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything advanced, treat strength as the base, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 41). Inference: the closing rule extends "teach before load" to machines, which staff often treat as needing no teaching.

**When NOT to apply** — Each bullet is the authors' biomechanical judgment; only the 90% figure carries a citation, so `untested`. The authors say "The above list is by no means complete." The 90% figure here is seated versus standing ("seated pressing or lifting exercises impose larger stresses on the lumbar spine than their standing equivalents (as much as 90% more, Chaffin & Andersson, 1984)", PDF 481 / p.470); the 4.2.7 entry gives the same source's 90% for a seated back allowed to flex forward ([[heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use]]). Inference: these are two framings of one cited source, and this entry has not checked which is the original's. Machines built since the book may not share these design faults; check the machine in front of you rather than the category. # A Machine That Stops One Joint Moving Usually Raises the Stress on the Joints Next to It

**What it is** — The last bullet of the 8.10 machine list: "It is important to know that, if a machine prevents any joint from moving, then there will usually be an increase in stress on adjacent joints. For instance, the seated leg extension machine tends to immobilise the hip joint, so that greater stress falls on the nearby knee joint. Similarly spinal stress generally increases for all machines which compel you to push against a load in a seated position. Besides changing to equivalent free weights exercises, you could carefully control the speed and transition accelerations throughout such exercises" (PDF 483 / p.472, checked against the page image). A companion bullet: "any machine which requires you to sit prevents you from using your hip, knee and ankle joints to absorb shock or redistribute loading" (PDF 482 / p.471).

**Why it works** — In a free standing movement the load is shared and redistributed across a chain of joints; fix one link and the neighbouring joint takes what it would have shed. The seated-back-extension bullet gives the same reasoning for the spine: "the seated position does not allow the hip and knee joints any freedom to modify the magnitude or direction of loading on the lower back," so it "can impose a greater compressive and transverse loading on lower spinal structures than an equivalent deadlift" (PDF 481 / p.470).

**When to apply** — Before choosing a machine exercise, ask which joints it fixes and which joint sits next to them; that neighbour is where the extra stress goes. Two remedies from the page: switch to the free-weight equivalent, or control speed and "transition accelerations." Useful when an athlete reports knee pain on leg extensions or back pain on seated presses.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors say "usually," not always, and give no measurements, so `untested`. Inference: in rehabilitation, fixing a joint on purpose to protect it or to isolate a weak muscle can be the right call; the principle says where the cost lands, not that the cost is never worth paying. The 4.2.7 entry already gives the leg-extension knee-shear example with its reasoning ([[heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use]]); this entry is the general rule the 8.10 list states.

**Example** — The authors' own: the seated leg extension "tends to immobilise the hip joint, so that greater stress falls on the nearby knee joint" (PDF 483 / p.472).

**Related** — [[framework--machine-safety-checklist-hazards-and-countermeasures]], [[heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use]] (4.2.7: seated knee extension and knee shear)

# What Decides Whether Muscles Protect a Joint: Reflexes, Eccentric Qualities, Coordination, Connective Tissue, and the Initial State at Loading

**What it is** — The authors: "Protection by the muscles is a function of the various extensor reflexes and the characteristics of the eccentric strength of the relevant muscles. It depends on many factors including starting strength, how rapidly the muscles are recruited to contract (the quality of reactive ability discussed in Section 5.3.3), the efficiency of coordinated action by appropriate muscle groups, the strength of the eccentric contraction, eccentric endurance, isometric strength and strength endurance after movement ceases, strength-flexibility, the elasticity of the muscle complex and the strength of the connective tissues involved" (PDF 483 / p.472, checked against the page image). A second dimension is timing: "The protective process also depends on the initial state of the major stabilisers and movers involved when the threatening load is imposed on the body. This load may be imposed on a part supported by isometric, concentric or eccentric movement, or even on a part completely at rest. In other words, depending on initial conditions at the moment of loading, adequacy of protection will be determined by isometric strength and endurance, and concentric or eccentric strength, strength-speed and strength-endurance, as well as by overflow or compensatory muscle activity to furnish supplementary support for the major stabilisers and movers" (PDF 483 / p.472).

**Why it works** — Because protection depends on so many qualities and on the state the joint is in when the load arrives, no single quality can be trained to cover it. The authors draw that conclusion: "General strength training on its own is inadequate to guarantee improved muscular protection for the body. The large range of processes implicated in musculoskeletal protection emphasizes the importance of special strength training in the properly-sequenced, multi-faceted manner discussed earlier in this book" (PDF 483 / p.472).

**When to apply** — As a checklist when a programme's stated aim is injury resilience: count which of the listed qualities it trains (starting strength, reactive ability, eccentric strength and endurance, isometric strength after movement stops, strength-flexibility, connective tissue) and in which initial states (moving, holding, at rest). Inference: the "part completely at rest" case argues for some training where load arrives unexpectedly on a relaxed or holding limb, not only on a muscle already braced.

**When NOT to apply** — The list is the authors' synthesis with no study attached, so `untested`. It names qualities, not tests or doses. It is about protection under imposed load and does not rank the factors. "Overflow or compensatory muscle activity" is the same irradiation idea the book uses elsewhere; it is not separately evidenced here.

**Example** — Inference: a defensive back hit while planting (eccentric state) needs eccentric strength and reactive recruitment; the same player hit while standing still needs isometric strength and quick onset. The authors' list covers both through "initial conditions at the moment of loading" (PDF 483 / p.472).

**Related** — [[claim--strong-muscles-protect-joints-only-when-contracted-in-the-right-pattern]], [[claim--ligaments-carry-more-load-than-muscles-under-joint-traction-basmajian]], [[principle--condition-tendons-ligaments-and-bone-not-only-muscle]]

# Fig 8.10: A Fuzzy-Logic Model Linking Exercise Intensity or Duration to the Blend of the Three Energy Systems

**What it is** — The authors give "An example of how fuzzy logic may be used to explain the relationship between the duration (or intensity) of activity at any moment to the contributions of the three main energy processes in the body (see 1.14)" (PDF 487 / p.476, checked against the page image). Fig 8.10, read from the page image (PDF 488 / p.477): the X axis is "EXERCISE INTENSITY," drawn as five overlapping fuzzy sets, Very low, Low, Medium, High, Very high, beside a vertical arrow "DURATION OF ACTIVITY" running from Long (top) to Brief (bottom). The Y axis is "RATE OF ENERGY PRODUCTION," drawn as three overlapping bell-shaped sets, Very Rapid, Intermediate, Slow, labelled underneath as HIGH ENERGY PHOSPHAGENS, NON-OXIDATIVE GLYCOLYTIC, OXIDATIVE GLYCOLYTIC. Three rules link them: "If X very low Then Y slow," "If X medium Then Y intermediate," "If X very high Then Y very rapid," each drawn as a fuzzy patch on a curve labelled "Y = F(X)." The caption: "The application of fuzzy logic to understanding the dependence of the intensity (or duration) of any exercise on the three major metabolic processes. The method uses rules that relate fuzzy sets of rates of energy production such as 'very rapid' to fuzzy sets of exercise duration such as 'very short'. The relationship between the X and Y sets produces a chain of fuzzy patches, which can approximate a performance curve Y = F(X)" (PDF 488 / p.477).

**Why it works** — The authors: "This model emphasizes that optimal efficiency for any given duration (or intensity) of exercise depends on the concurrent different contributions of the short, intermediate and long-term energy systems. This enables us to think less in terms of one activity being aerobic and another anaerobic, and to plan training so that the dynamic balance between the three energy mechanisms is shifted in the most appropriate direction for any given sport" (PDF 487 / p.476). The overlapping sets are the point: at any intensity more than one system contributes.

**When to apply** — Conditioning design for mixed-demand sports: describe each drill by where it sits on the intensity or duration axis and which blend it shifts toward, rather than labelling it "aerobic" or "anaerobic." Useful when teaching staff that energy systems overlap.

**When NOT to apply** — The figure is schematic: no times, intensities or percentage contributions are given, so it cannot be used to set work-rest ratios, and the entry is `untested`. The caption and figure do not match exactly: the caption speaks of duration sets "such as 'very short'," while the figure labels its sets by intensity (Very low to Very high) and marks duration only as an arrow from Long to Brief; no set is labelled "very short." Inference: the figure treats intensity and duration as the same axis run in opposite directions, which holds for maximal efforts but not for submaximal work that is both long and moderate. The text layer reads the curve label as "Y « F(X)"; the image shows "Y = F(X)."

**Example** — Rule three of the figure: "If X very high Then Y very rapid," with the Very Rapid set sitting over HIGH ENERGY PHOSPHAGENS (PDF 488 / p.477). Inference: a brief maximal sprint draws mostly on phosphagens, with the overlapping glycolytic set still contributing.

**Related** — [[claim--physiological-thresholds-are-ranges-and-athletes-regulate-performance-by-feel]], [[claim--non-equilibrium-and-self-organisation-prigogine-as-a-model-for-performance-leaps]]

# Fig 8.10: A Fuzzy-Logic Model Linking Exercise Intensity or Duration to the Blend of the Three Energy Systems

**What it is** — The authors give "An example of how fuzzy logic may be used to explain the relationship between the duration (or intensity) of activity at any moment to the contributions of the three main energy processes in the body (see 1.14)" (PDF 487 / p.476, checked against the page image); the book's "(see 1.14)" is a misprint: in this edition 1.14 is Neurophysiological Aspects of Exercise and 1.15 is Bioenergetics and the Energy Systems (table of contents, PDF 4). Fig 8.10, read from the page image (PDF 488 / p.477): the X axis is "EXERCISE INTENSITY," drawn as five overlapping fuzzy sets, Very low, Low, Medium, High, Very high, beside a vertical arrow "DURATION OF ACTIVITY" running from Long (top) to Brief (bottom). The Y axis is "RATE OF ENERGY PRODUCTION," drawn as three overlapping bell-shaped sets, Very Rapid, Intermediate, Slow, labelled underneath as HIGH ENERGY PHOSPHAGENS, NON-OXIDATIVE GLYCOLYTIC, OXIDATIVE GLYCOLYTIC. Three rules link them: "If X very low Then Y slow," "If X medium Then Y intermediate," "If X very high Then Y very rapid," each drawn as a fuzzy patch on a curve labelled "Y = F(X)." The caption: "The application of fuzzy logic to understanding the dependence of the intensity (or duration) of any exercise on the three major metabolic processes. The method uses rules that relate fuzzy sets of rates of energy production such as 'very rapid' to fuzzy sets of exercise duration such as 'very short'. The relationship between the X and Y sets produces a chain of fuzzy patches, which can approximate a performance curve Y = F(X)" (PDF 488 / p.477).

**Why it works** — The authors: "This model emphasizes that optimal efficiency for any given duration (or intensity) of exercise depends on the concurrent different contributions of the short, intermediate and long-term energy systems. This enables us to think less in terms of one activity being aerobic and another anaerobic, and to plan training so that the dynamic balance between the three energy mechanisms is shifted in the most appropriate direction for any given sport" (PDF 487 / p.476). The overlapping sets are the point: at any intensity more than one system contributes.

**When to apply** — Conditioning design for mixed-demand sports: describe each drill by where it sits on the intensity or duration axis and which blend it shifts toward, rather than labelling it "aerobic" or "anaerobic." Useful when teaching staff that energy systems overlap.

**When NOT to apply** — The figure is schematic: no times, intensities or percentage contributions are given, so it cannot be used to set work-rest ratios, and the entry is `untested`. The caption and figure do not match exactly: the caption speaks of duration sets "such as 'very short'," while the figure labels its sets by intensity (Very low to Very high) and marks duration only as an arrow from Long to Brief; no set is labelled "very short." Inference: the figure treats intensity and duration as the same axis run in opposite directions, which holds for maximal efforts but not for submaximal work that is both long and moderate. The text layer reads the curve label as "Y « F(X)"; the image shows "Y = F(X)."

**Example** — Rule three of the figure: "If X very high Then Y very rapid," with the Very Rapid set sitting over HIGH ENERGY PHOSPHAGENS (PDF 488 / p.477). Inference: a brief maximal sprint draws mostly on phosphagens, with the overlapping glycolytic set still contributing.

# Classic Energy-System Percentage Tables by Sport (Fox & Mathews, 1974): Football Listed at ~90% Phosphagen

**What it is** — The authors reproduce Fox & Mathews' (1974) classic tables (Table 1.4)
estimating the percentage contribution of the short-term (phosphagen/ATP-CP), intermediate
(non-oxidative glycolytic), and long-term (oxidative/aerobic) energy systems to different
training modes and sports. American football is listed at 90% short-term, 10%
intermediate, 0% long-term, among the most phosphagen-dominant sports in the table,
comparable to golf (95/5/0) and volleyball (90/10/0), and far more phosphagen-dominant
than field hockey or soccer half-backs (60/20/20). The authors themselves caution that
"figures for longer duration events such as the 1500m run have been modified by other
researchers and their accuracy needs to be re-examined," that "the highly determinate
nature of this whole scheme, compiled several decades ago, has been questioned more
recently," and that it should not be used casually because it disguises moment-to-moment
metabolic demand shifts within a single sport (printed 81). (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp.
80-81.)

**Why it works** — The authors state these figures "reflect the average contributions made
by three concurrently operating metabolic systems ... for an average athlete," which
"disguises the fact ... that the metabolic demands often differ from instant to instant
during every type of activity taking place in each sport" (printed 81). Inference: for
football specifically, actual play consists of short high-intensity bursts (plays)
separated by long rest (huddles, substitutions), so an average figure can obscure the real
repeated-sprint, phosphagen-dominant-per-play structure while also underweighting the role
of aerobic recovery between bursts; the text does not itself apply this reasoning to
football.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's stated conditioning priority for
football is alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp and game demands, with
glycolytic conditioning treated as a "worst case scenario" absorbed incidentally rather
than programmed as a primary target (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39`); the baseline also states the aerobic
system's main value for speed-power athletes is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP
between bouts), not distance capacity (citing `2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md
p.9`). **Inference:** this table's 90/10/0 split for football (near-zero credited to the
long-term/aerobic system) looks, at first read, to be in tension with the baseline's
explicit inclusion of aerobic capacity as a Goal-1 priority for football, but the tension
likely resolves once "aerobic system" is understood functionally: the baseline treats
aerobic fitness as enabling faster ATP/phosphagen regeneration between the very
phosphagen-dominant plays this table describes, not as a source of in-play energy. Read
together, not as contradictory: this table describes what fuels a single play; the
baseline describes what determines how well that fuel regenerates for the next one.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors' own caution applies directly here: **Inference:** do
not use the 90/10/0 football figure as a precise or current number; it is a decades-old
average estimate for the sport as a whole, not a modern, position-specific or play-by-play
breakdown. The text itself states that "the highly determinate nature of this whole scheme,
compiled several decades ago, has been questioned more recently" and that figures for
longer events "have been modified by other researchers" (printed 81). This entry is rated
`contested` beyond that self-flagged caution because modern measurement puts the aerobic
contribution far higher, and earlier in an effort, than these 1970s tables allow for (e.g.
Gastin, 2001, Sports Med 31:725-741).

**Example** — **Inference:** a single football play (a few seconds of maximal effort)
draws almost entirely on the phosphagen system, consistent with the table; but the
athlete's ability to repeat that near-maximal output play after play, series after series,
depends heavily on aerobic capacity for recovery between plays (the quality the baseline
prioritizes).

# Under Joint Traction, Ligaments Carry More Load Than Is Believed Unless the Muscles Are Consciously Recruited (Basmajian)

**What it is** — The authors: "Basmajian (1978) reports that *ligaments play a much greater part in supporting loads than is generally believed, unless conscious effort is made to recruit the relevant muscles*. In most situations where traction is exerted across a joint, muscles appear to play only a secondary role to ligaments. Thus, deadlifts, toe-touches and 'aerobic' activities involving flexion and rotation of the spine may rely more on the spinal ligaments than the erector spinae in stabilising the spine. Training to increase ligament hypertrophy and strength thus would appear to be just as important as muscle strengthening" (PDF 483 / p.472, checked against the page image; italics in the original). They add: "Basmajian also questions the validity of 'ligamento-muscular protective reflexes', since reflex muscle activity often fails to occur when a limb is loaded. Apparently a great deal still has to be learned about the mechanics of neuromuscular action" (PDF 484 / p.473, checked against the page image; the clipped left-margin letters of "often" and "neuromuscular" are partly reconstructed).

**Why it works** — Under traction (a pull across the joint), passive tissue is already in line with the load, and muscle joins only if recruited. Inference: the qualifier "unless conscious effort is made" is what makes this a coaching point; deliberate bracing changes who carries the load.

**When to apply** — Programming for spinal flexion and rotation exposure (deadlifts, toe-touches, the page's "aerobic" activities): cue deliberate muscle recruitment, and treat connective-tissue conditioning as a training aim in its own right.

**When NOT to apply** — Basmajian (1978) is cited, not described (no method or data on the page), so `untested`. "Training to increase ligament hypertrophy" is the authors' "would appear," a hedge, and the page gives no method for it. Inference: the deadlift line can be misread as "deadlifts are ligament exercises"; the 3.7 entry gives the book's fuller account that a skilled lifter balances muscle and ligament load and that heavy spinal flexion can damage discs ([[claim--spinal-ligaments-share-load-with-erector-spinae-in-heavy-pulls]]). The reflex point is about limbs under load and is stated as a question, not a finding.

**Example** — The authors' own list of activities that "may rely more on the spinal ligaments than the erector spinae": "deadlifts, toe-touches and 'aerobic' activities involving flexion and rotation of the spine" (PDF 483 / p.472).

**Related** — [[claim--spinal-ligaments-share-load-with-erector-spinae-in-heavy-pulls]] (3.7), [[principle--condition-tendons-ligaments-and-bone-not-only-muscle]] (8.2), [[claim--strong-muscles-protect-joints-only-when-contracted-in-the-right-pattern]], [[claim--limb-loading-fatigue-is-often-ligament-and-capsule-tension-not-muscle-fatigue]]

# What Actually Stabilizes a Joint Changes as It Approaches End-Range

**What it is** — Against the "widespread opinion that muscles act as efficient synergistic
stabilisers," the authors argue muscle cannot always respond quickly enough to protect a
joint against a large, rapid (particularly torsional) impact (Pope et al., 1978), and
propose joint stabilization instead works in a sequence:
1. The contractile element (activated by the stretch reflex complex) together with the
muscle's series elastic component (SEC) act as primary stabilizers, if the loading rate
allows the muscle to respond in time.
2. If the joint reaches the physical limits of muscle length, strength, or endurance,
protection shifts to the ligaments and the SEC; if the inverse stretch reflex (GTO) signals
the muscle to relax at its maximum length, the muscle's parallel elastic component (PEC)
also contributes to stabilization. Receptors resembling Golgi tendon organs have been found
on the surface of cruciate ligaments (Schultz et al., 1984), and muscles show reflex
contraction if ligaments are stretched to the point of pain (Basmajian, 1978).
3. If the joint is extended to its limit without sufficient muscle contraction, primary
stabilization is provided by ligaments and the PEC; once the initial latency period for
muscle excitation passes, the contracting muscle and its SEC contribute as secondary
stabilizers.
4. In certain joints, skeletal structure itself can act as the final stabilizer at the
limits of joint movement.
(PDF p. 193, printed p. 182.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no derivation for the four-stage sequence itself; they
present it as "probably more accurate" than the "widespread opinion" it replaces, without
showing the reasoning step by step. Inference: the sequence is consistent with the
mechanical roles already established for the SEC, PEC, and stretch/inverse-stretch reflexes
elsewhere in the text (see [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] and
[[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]]), combined
with the cited finding that ligaments themselves carry GTO-like tension receptors (Schultz
et al., 1984) and can trigger protective muscle contraction (Basmajian, 1978), but the book
does not walk through this derivation itself.

**When to apply** — Use this sequence to explain why a joint can be injured even with
strong, well-conditioned muscles around it: at high loading rates (stage 1's premise
fails), stabilization falls to ligament and PEC tissue that may not be conditioned to the
same standard as the muscle. The authors' own framing supports this: "the necessity for
appropriately conditioning all the interacting soft tissues again becomes obvious" (printed
182), reframing injury-prevention conditioning as needing to address ligament/capsule
tissue specifically, not only muscular strength.

**When NOT to apply** — This is the authors' synthesized model, not a single cited
experimental finding; treat the four numbered stages as an organizing framework for
reasoning about joint stabilization, not as a validated, measured sequence with defined
timing thresholds. Confidence is capped at `supported` because the sequence itself
(as opposed to the individual cited facts feeding it) is not independently attributed to a
specific study.

**Example** — Inference: a sudden, high-velocity valgus torque to the knee arrives faster
than stage 1's muscular response can engage, meaning stages 2-3 (ligament and PEC) bear
more of the load than they would under a slower, anticipated movement. This is consistent

unanticipated rather than caused by direct impact (see vault

on non-contact ACL mechanisms); the book gives no ACL-specific example itself.

# Attitude and Goal-Specific Visualisation Change Strength and Speed; No Prescription Works Unless the Mind Lets the Body Use It

**What it is** — Under "Non-Physical Factors" the authors write that "the central role played by non-physical factors must never be forgotten. Autogenic training, visualisation, hypnosis, biofeedback, motivational techniques and other psychological methods have formed an integral part of Russian and Eastern European training for many years," and that "even the most meticulous prescription of all the training means and methods in this book will not guarantee success unless the mind enables the body to utilise its full potential during training, restoration and competition" (PDF 484 / p.473, checked against the page image; the left margin is clipped, and "At", "visualisation", "integral", "the most" and "unless" are partly reconstructed). Evidence offered: "it has repeatedly been shown that one's attitude during training or competition has a profound effect on physical performance"; "Highly motivated subjects will usually produce superior performances, especially in the presence of spectators"; "*Visualisation techniques which require the athlete to fervently concentrate on accelerating the training load can increase power and speed of movement*"; and "athletes performed loadless weightlifting movements with a broomstick while imagining effort against maximal loads revealed improvements in strength and skill (Kovalik, 1978)" (PDF 484 / p.473, italics in the original). They predict that "highly motivated, mood-linked, goal-specific visualisation (or 'imagineering')" will "become recognised as a vital part of modern training" (PDF 484 / p.473).

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism on this page beyond motivation and concentration. Inference: the "accelerating the training load" wording ties visualisation to intent to move fast, the same target as compensatory acceleration; the broomstick study ties imagined maximal effort to real strength gains without load.

**When to apply** — Add a goal-specific cue to heavy or explosive sets ("drive the bar as fast as you can"), and use imagined maximal effort with an unloaded bar or stick when load is not available or not wanted. The authors point readers to specialised texts, naming "the extensive survey by Murphy and White (1978) of altered states associated with outstanding performances in different sports" (PDF 484 / p.473). Eric's review: "Constraints-led and external-cue coaching are not part of Eric's practice. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q25): 'I don't apply it, as I don't fully understand it. I want to know more.'" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 170). Inference: an "accelerate the load" cue is a cue about the bar, so it sits near the external-cue methods Eric names as a learning area, not in his current practice.

**When NOT to apply** — Only Kovalik (1978) is cited, and only by name; "repeatedly been shown" has no references, so `untested`. The authors limit their own claim on the same page: it "does not imply invoking the vague notions of mind-body power which are helping to market hundreds of self-development courses of dubious validity," whose success "has a great deal to do with the placebo effect (or faith factor)" (PDF 484 / p.473). The steroid sentence ("The increase in aggression by anabolic steroids is also regarded as one of the reasons why these drugs can improve performance") is reported as a view, not a recommendation. The authors also note attitude is "a complicating factor when one attempts to compare the research done on different subjects by different scientists under different conditions."

**Example** — Kovalik (1978), as the authors give it: loadless weightlifting movements with a broomstick while imagining maximal loads improved "strength and skill" (PDF 484 / p.473).

# Emotional State, Hypnosis, and an Audience Can Each Change Measured Strength

**What it is** — The authors report several psychological effects on strength expression.
The numeric effects (the fourfold emotion figure, and the 22.5%/31.7% hypnosis figures) each
rest on one citation; the group and spectator effects each cite several studies spanning
1924-1965. Before these, the authors state that the "motor objective" set by the situation
and the coach's instructions prepares the athlete's body for the forthcoming action, forming
"tuners" that are a prerequisite for successful performance (Ozolin, 1949; Shoikhet, 1966;
Eremin, 1968, printed 170). Strong positive emotions can immediately increase the energy of
muscular contraction by as much as four times (Vinogradov, 1966). Under certain conditions,
hypnosis has been shown to increase muscular strength by 22.5% and to decrease it by 31.7%
(Ikai & Steinhaus, 1961); the authors give no detail on what conditions produced which
direction. Group activities produce greater results than individual activities (Gurnee,
1937; Abel, 1938; Weyner & Zeaman, 1956; Beasley, 1958; Cratty, 1965). The presence of
spectators also increases the effectiveness of motor activity (Gates, 1924; Lazaruc et al,
1952; Cratty & Hutten, 1964), with novices showing a significantly greater improvement from
an audience than advanced athletes (Singer, 1965). The authors' summary: "carefully directed
training creates a specific emotional background which makes strength work more
productive." (PDF pp. 181-182, printed pp. 170-171, "3.4.7 Emotion and Other Psychological
Factors.")

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism connecting emotion, hypnosis, or social
presence to measured force output beyond naming the findings themselves. Inference: these
are most plausibly framed as changes in voluntary activation or willingness to approach the
true physiological ceiling (raising the "expressed" fraction of maximal strength) rather
than a change in the muscle's underlying contractile capacity, but the source does not state
this explanation.

**When to apply** — Inference: the book gives no applied protocol. The motor-objective/
"tuner" point (situation and coach instruction shaping readiness, printed 170) is the more
actionable of the two threads here and fits ordinary pre-lift coaching cueing and
competition-day environment management; the hypnosis and raw emotion figures are not
actionable coaching levers, only documented phenomena.

**When NOT to apply** — The numeric hypnosis and emotion figures each rest on a single
citation, with no magnitude-reproducing modern study named; do not treat the 22.5%/31.7%
hypnosis figures or the fourfold emotion figure as established, reproducible effect sizes.
The group and spectator effects rest on several older citations (1924-1965), which is a
broader evidence base than a single study but still no modern replication. Hypnosis for
performance manipulation is not a documented Baylor Applied Performance or Athletic
Performance practice and raises consent and oversight questions this source does not
address; this entry documents the claim, it does not endorse using hypnosis as an
intervention. The social-facilitation effect is explicitly reported as larger in novices
than advanced athletes, so it should not be assumed to transfer to elite competitors
unchanged.

**Example** — Inference: a coach who has observed that certain athletes perform noticeably
better in a full weight room with teammates present than alone is consistent with the
group/spectator findings above, though the book gives no team-sport or strength-training
example of its own.

**Related** — None found in the staging library or vault; this is a distinct angle from
[[heuristic--instruction-type-and-verbal-framing-shape-strength-output]] (same source
subsection, coaching-instruction effects rather than emotional/social state effects).

# Farfel et al (1975): Even Elite Weightlifters Misjudged the Force They Were Exerting, With Errors of Up to 100% Common

**What it is** — The authors introduce it with a principle (in italics on the page): "*The production and control of muscular force is one of the primary tasks in all sport*, a process which relies on kinaesthetic awareness of what is happening within the musculoskeletal system in response to events in the sporting environment" (PDF 490 / p.479, checked against the page image). Then the study: "Farfel et al (1975) set out to ascertain the type of information upon which this motor control is based by examining the ability of weightlifters to estimate the forces which they exert during different lifts and different stages of various lifts (Sokolov, 1982). After studying a group of elite Russian weightlifters (Masters of Sport Class), they concluded that the ability of even world class weightlifters to estimate the force (relative to their experience of what a 1RM load feels like) they are exerting at different stages of the Olympic lifts under static and explosive conditions is very poor. Measurements made on special pulling dynamometers showed that errors of as much as 100% were common" (PDF 490 / p.479).

**Why it works** — The study's own explanation: "It was concluded that this weakness in being able to accurately control force is the result of inappropriate training methods and that the lifters needed to systematically perfect their 'muscle sense', both by developing an acute inner feel for kinaesthetic processes and by using biofeedback information from specialised dynamometers to enable them to quantitatively imprint this awareness" (PDF 490 / p.479).

**When to apply** — When a programme relies on an athlete's sense of effort to set or adjust load: this result says even elite lifters' estimates of force can be badly off. Use measured feedback (bar velocity, force plate or dynamometer readouts) to calibrate the feel, as the study recommends. Eric's review: the baseline chose mRSI from daily CMJ testing because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74). Inference: Farfel's result is a parallel case for measured over felt indicators, though Farfel tested force estimation within lifts, not daily readiness.

**When NOT to apply** — The population (elite Masters of Sport) and instrument (special pulling dynamometers) are named, and the conditions (static and explosive, different lift stages, relative to 1RM feel) are stated, so `supported` under the standard the 8c review applied to partly described Vorobyev data; but no n, no error distribution and no protocol are given, and the study is reported second-hand through Sokolov (1982). "As much as 100%" is an upper figure described as "common," not a mean. The cause ("inappropriate training methods") is the study authors' conclusion, not tested. Inference: this does not contradict RPE-based training; it says the felt scale needs calibrating, which is what the authors propose.

**Example** — Elite Russian weightlifters, asked to estimate their force at different stages of the Olympic lifts against their sense of a 1RM, made errors "of as much as 100%" on special pulling dynamometers (PDF 490 / p.479).

# Keep Everyone Who Works With an Athlete in Regular Contact, and Treat the Massage Therapist's Hands as an Early Overtraining Detector

**What it is** — In "Application of New Methods" the authors report that, because constant use of the same massage "can diminish its benefits or even inhibit performance," "Russian coaches recommend *partial restoration* and *limited zone massage*, at the same time communicating regularly with the massage specialists who work with their athletes. These specialists can usually manually detect in the soft tissues of athletes that may be of great relevance in the early diagnosis of overtraining or unbalanced training" (PDF 488 / p.477, checked against the page image; the sentence is printed with a word missing after "detect"). The general rule: "An important implication of this is that it is essential for all personnel working with an athlete in any way whatsoever to keep in regular contact to ensure that all training programmes are properly monitored and modified, if necessary" (PDF 488 / p.477). They add that "all Russian coaches and physical education coaches spend 700-900 hours over several semesters learning and practising sports massage."

**Why it works** — The therapist's hands sample the tissue several times a week, so changes in tone or tenderness can show before performance drops. The kinaesthetic section later describes the same practice: "massage specialists used their hands to palpate the muscles and other soft tissues to identify patterns of tension and development in the bodies of their athletes," and "The results were communicated to coaches" (PDF 489-490 / pp.478-479).

**When to apply** — Build a short, regular channel between soft-tissue staff and the strength and sport coaches (a weekly note on tone, tenderness or asymmetry per athlete). Use it as one input to load decisions, alongside objective tests. Eric's review: "The athlete is described as the hub of a wheel, with every support function (academics, Athletic Medicine, nutrition, mental health, Applied Performance) as a spoke" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 48; the line continues past a dash that no single discipline owns the athlete's development). Inference: the authors' "all personnel ... keep in regular contact" is that wheel put into practice.

**When NOT to apply** — No validation of palpation as an overtraining marker is given, so `untested`. # Teaching a Skill in Reverse Order, or in Components, Beat Natural-Sequence Teaching: the Snatch Learned From the Drop Backwards Was 40 Percent More Effective

**What it is** — Under "Advances in Methods of Coaching" the authors write: "Sometimes, apparently logical methods of learning are not necessarily found to be the most effective. For instance, Russian researchers have discovered that teaching a new movement in its natural sequential order from start to finish is not necessarily as effective as *teaching the action in the reverse order* (Vorobyev, 1978). They found that learning of the Olympic weightlifting snatch from the final drop phase backwards to the starting pull is 40 percent more effective than the conventional order of learning. They also examined the effect of breaking sporting movements down into basic components and having athletes learn each element separately before attempting the whole movement. This method of *component learning* also proved to be superior to the conventional method of natural sequence learning" (PDF 490-491 / pp.479-480, checked against the page images; italics in the original).

**Why it works** — The page gives no mechanism. The authors frame it under motor learning: "An understanding of how to programme the human biocomputer effectively by sensory and motor activity is vital to the growth of performance," given that "structure and function in the central nervous system is not as rigidly determined as hitherto thought (Ch 1: under 'Neural Changes with Training')" (PDF 490 / p.479). Inference: starting from the receiving position means every later practice of the earlier phases ends in a position already learned, so the lifter always finishes in a familiar place.

**When to apply** — Teaching the snatch (and likely the clean and jerk) to novices: begin with the overhead squat and receiving position, then add the drop, then the pull, ending with the full lift from the floor. Use component practice where a whole skill is too complex to learn at once. Eric's review: the baseline's operating value includes "teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything advanced" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 41). Inference: reverse-order teaching is one way to order those basic positions within a lift.

**When NOT to apply** — "40 percent more effective" has no stated measure (speed of learning, technique rating, load lifted), no sample and no follow-up on the page; Vorobyev (1978) is cited, not described, so `untested`. The component-learning result has no number at all. Inference: the result is for a closed skill with a fixed end position; open, reactive skills may not break down the same way.

# A Lifting Belt Does Not Keep the Back Flat; Its Real Value Is a Proprioceptive Cue for Occasional Maximal Attempts

**What it is** — The authors open 8.9.1 with the two camps: belt users claim "it definitely supports the back"; non-users say "their backs are strong enough not to rely on external support," and "Some authorities regard the benefits of the belt to be mainly psychological" (PDF 478 / p.467, checked against the page image). Their answer: the claim that the belt keeps the back flat "is definitely not accurate, because we all see lifters rounding their backs even when they are wearing thick, wide belts. Strong muscles and not strong belts keep your back flat." But "In one sense, however, a belt can assist you in keeping your back flat - not by lending support, but rather by creating an awareness of the direction of curvature of your lower back," through proprioception. "For this reason alone, it is probably a good idea to wear a belt during occasional maximal attempts, although it is not a good idea to rely entirely on a belt without learning how to position your back correctly and tense the right muscles at the right time. Belts per se do not weaken the trunk musculature; it is only if one persists in relying on a tightly worn belt for long periods that this possibility may occur" (PDF 478 / p.467).

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism is sensory: "its pressure exerted on the skin and muscles below it tells you a lot about the tension in the muscles, the pressure in your abdomen and the straightness of your back" (PDF 478 / p.467). Relaxed back muscles, not the absence of a belt, are what load "the ligaments and intervertebral discs of your back. No amount of belt support is going to solve this problem" (PDF 478 / p.467).

**When to apply** — Occasional maximal attempts, where the belt's pressure gives the lifter feedback on back curvature and abdominal pressure. Later in the chapter the book points back to "The correct use of the weightlifting belt in proprioceptive lifting training or enhancing trunk stability, sometimes in conjunction with strain measuring devices" (PDF 489 / p.478). Eric's review: the baseline's stated operating value is "safety first, keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything advanced, treat strength as the base, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 41). Inference: the authors' order (learn to position the back and tense the right muscles first, belt only as an occasional cue) fits that sequence.

**When NOT to apply** — Not as routine support on every set: the authors' own caution is against relying "on a tightly worn belt for long periods." No study is cited for any belt claim on this page; the evidence offered is the observation that belted lifters still round their backs, so `untested`. The "weakens the trunk" point is stated as a possibility only ("this possibility may occur"), not as a finding. Note the page's own typo: "helps keeps the flat" (PDF 478), where "back" is missing.

**Example** — The authors' observation: lifters "rounding their backs even when they are wearing thick, wide belts" (PDF 478 / p.467), so the belt did not hold the back flat; the muscles have to.
